Exactly rounded sum

Source: R/xsum.R
xsum.Rd

xsum() adds its arguments exactly and rounds once, to the nearest double (ties to even). The result is the correctly rounded value of the true sum, so it does not depend on the order of the elements, on the platform, or on whether R was built with long doubles. Base sum() accumulates in long double, which is 80-bit on x86-64 Linux and Windows and 64-bit on Apple Silicon, so its result varies between machines.

Usage

xsum(..., na.rm = FALSE)

Arguments

...

Numeric, integer, logical or complex vectors, or NULL.

na.rm

Remove NA and NaN values before summing?

Value

A double of length one, or a complex if any argument is complex.

Details

Integers and logicals are converted to double exactly; the result is always a double, or a complex if any argument is complex. Complex values are summed as two exact sums, of the real and of the imaginary parts.

Special values

With na.rm = FALSE, the rules are the same on every platform:

Input containsResult
nothing0
any NANA
no NA, any other NaNNaN
both Inf and -InfNaN
Inf (and finite values)Inf
-Inf (and finite values)-Inf
finite values whose exact sum is out of rangeInf or -Inf
only zeros, of any sign0 (never -0)

na.rm = TRUE removes NA and NaN, as sum() does; infinities stay. For complex input, each part follows the table, and an element is removed when either of its parts is NA or NaN.

See also

zuexact_info() for the build's accumulator threshold.

Examples

# Base sum() gives 1 on x86-64 and 0 on Apple Silicon; xsum() gives 1.
xsum(c(1e16, 1, -1e16))
#> [1] 1

# Neither platform's sum() gets this one right.
sum(c(1e20, 1, -1e20))
#> [1] 0
xsum(c(1e20, 1, -1e20))
#> [1] 1

# The order of the terms never matters.
x <- c(1, 1e100, 1, -1e100)
xsum(x) == xsum(rev(x))
#> [1] TRUE

# Several arguments are summed together.
xsum(1:10, c(0.5, 0.25), TRUE)
#> [1] 56.75
